chapterNote: Chapter 27 gathers loose proverbs on the texture of real relationships — friendship that wounds to heal, praise that must come from another's mouth, the steadying friction of one life rubbed against another. It opens by puncturing self-confidence about tomorrow (v.1) and self-praise (v.2), and turns repeatedly to the friend: better an open rebuke than hidden love (v.5), faithful are a friend's wounds (v.6), iron sharpens iron (v.17). Threaded through are the heavier folly of the fool (vv.3, 22), the misery of the contentious wife (vv.15-16), the unfillable hunger of the human eye (v.20), and the testing of a man by his praise (v.21). It closes with a sustained pastoral charge (vv.23-27): tend your flocks diligently, for wealth is fleeting but honest husbandry feeds a household for generations.

1.text: Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a single day may bring to birth.
1.amp: Do not boast [halal — to praise, to make a shining display of yourself] about tomorrow [machar], for you do not know [yada] what a day [yom] may bring forth [yalad — to bear, to give birth].
1.notes: yalad (H3205) is the verb for giving birth — the day is pictured as pregnant with an outcome no man can foresee, so the boast of halal (H1984) over the unborn future is empty presumption (cf. Jas 4:13-16). The same root halal that rightly praises God here turns sour as self-praise about a day not yet delivered.

2.text: Let the praise of you rise from another's mouth, never from your own; let a stranger speak it, never your own lips.
2.amp: Let another [zur — one outside yourself, a stranger] praise [halal] you, and not your own mouth [peh]; a stranger [nokri — a foreigner, one with no stake in flattering you], and not your own lips [saphah].
2.notes: the doubled call for outside witness — zur (H2114) and nokri (H5237) — makes the point twice: praise has worth only when it comes from a mouth that gains nothing by giving it. Self-praise (halal, H1984, again) is the counterfeit of honor; true honor is conferred, never claimed.

3.text: A stone is heavy and sand a dead weight, but a fool's provocation outweighs them both.
3.amp: A stone [even] is heavy, and the sand [chol] a burden; but a fool's [evil — the morally dense fool] vexation [kaas — provocation, grief, the anger he stirs up] is heavier [kaved] than them both.
3.notes: kaas (H3708) is both the fool's own anger and the grief he inflicts on others — a weight that crushes more than stone or sand. The evil (H191) is the thick-headed fool whose temper is an unbearable load to those who must carry him (cf. 27:22).

4.text: Wrath is cruel and anger an overwhelming flood — but who can stand before jealousy?
4.amp: Wrath [chemah — hot fury, like venom] is cruel [akzeriyyut — savage, merciless], and anger [aph — the flaring nostril, the snort of rage] is overwhelming; but who is able to stand [amad — hold his ground, endure] before jealousy [qinah — jealous zeal, the consuming passion of a wronged love]?
4.notes: chemah (H2534), aph (H639), and qinah (H7068) climb a ladder of intensity: hot fury and flaring rage are bad enough, but qinah — jealousy, the fierce passion of betrayed love — is the flood before which no one can stand (amad, H5975). The same word names both human envy and God's own jealousy for His people (cf. 6:34; Song 8:6).

5.text: Better an open rebuke than love that hides itself.
5.amp: Better is open [galah — uncovered, brought into the light] rebuke [tokachat — corrective reproof] than love [ahavah] that is hidden [satar — concealed, kept back].
5.notes: galah (H1540), to uncover, and satar (H5641), to conceal, are set as opposites: love that stays hidden does the friend no good, while honest tokachat (H8433) brought into the open is the truer kindness. A rebuke spoken is worth more than affection felt but never voiced (cf. Lev 19:17).

6.text: Faithful are the wounds of a friend, but the kisses of an enemy are lavish and false.
6.amp: Faithful [aman — trustworthy, reliable] are the wounds [petsa — the cut, the bruise] of a friend [from ahab, one who loves]; but the kisses [neshiqah] of an enemy [sane — one who hates] are profuse [deceitful, multiplied to flatter].
6.notes: aman (H539), the root of 'amen,' marks the friend's painful cut as trustworthy — it can be relied on because it is meant for good. The contrast is razor-sharp: a friend's wound heals, an enemy's heaped-up kisses betray. The wounds come from one who loves (ahab, H157); the kisses from one who hates (sane, H8130).

7.text: The well-fed soul tramples on honey, but to the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet.
7.amp: The full [sabea] soul [nephesh] loathes [bus — treads underfoot, despises] a honeycomb; but to the hungry [raeb] soul [nephesh], every bitter thing is sweet [matoq].
7.notes: bus (H947) is literally to tread down — the satisfied appetite spurns even honey, while hunger makes the bitter taste sweet (matoq, H4966). The nephesh (H5315), the whole craving self, sets its value by its emptiness, a parable of how need teaches gratitude that abundance dulls.

8.text: Like a bird that strays far from its nest is a man who strays from his place.
8.amp: As a bird [tsippor] that wanders [nadad — flits, flees, roams away] from her nest [qen], so is a man [ish] who wanders [nadad] from his place [maqom — his appointed standing, his home].
8.notes: nadad (H5074) is repeated for the bird and the man alike — the restless flutter of one who has left where he belongs. maqom (H4725) is more than a house; it is the man's rightful standing and station, and to abandon it leaves him as exposed as a fledgling far from the nest.

9.text: Oil and incense gladden the heart, and the sweetness of a friend is his counsel from the soul.
9.amp: Ointment [shemen — fragrant oil] and perfume [qetoreth — incense, the rising sweet smoke] rejoice [samach] the heart [leb]; so does the sweetness [metheq — the pleasantness] of a man's friend [rea — neighbor, companion] by hearty [nephesh — soul-deep] counsel [etsah — advice, plan].
9.notes: as shemen (H8081) and qetoreth (H7004) delight the senses, so the counsel of a true rea (H7453) delights the heart — and the Hebrew locates that sweetness in the nephesh (H5315), counsel that rises from the soul rather than the surface. etsah (H6098), advice given from the depths of friendship, is itself a fragrance.

10.text: Do not forsake your own friend or your father's friend, and do not go to your brother's house in the day of your calamity — better a neighbor near than a brother far away.
10.amp: Your own friend [rea], and your father's [ab] friend [rea], do not forsake [azab — abandon, let go]; and do not go [bo] into your brother's [ach] house [bayith] in the day [yom] of your calamity [eyd — disaster]: better [tov] is a neighbor [shaken] who is near [qarov] than a brother [ach] far off [rachoq].
10.notes: azab (H5800), to forsake, warns against trading old loyalty for new — the tested friend, even one's father's friend, outlasts the accident of kinship. In the day of eyd (H343), proximity proves more than blood: the qarov (H7138) neighbor who can reach you outweighs the rachoq (H7350) brother who cannot (cf. 18:24).

11.text: Be wise, my son, and gladden my heart, that I may have an answer for the one who taunts me.
11.amp: My son [ben], be wise [chakam — act with skill], and make my heart [leb] glad [samach], that I may answer [shub — turn back a word, return a reply] him who reproaches [taunts, scorns] me.
11.notes: a son's wisdom is a father's vindication: shub (H7725), to return, here means to send back an answer to the mocker, for a child who lives wisely is the standing reply to any who would scorn the parent's teaching (cf. 23:15-16). chakam (H2449) — to be wise — becomes the father's own honor.

12.text: The prudent man sees danger coming and takes cover, but the simple keep walking and pay the price.
12.amp: A prudent [arum — shrewd, clear-eyed] man foresees [raah — sees, perceives] the evil [ra — harm, danger], and hides [satar — takes shelter] himself; but the simple [peti — the naive, the heedless] pass on [abar — walk straight on], and are punished [anash — pay the penalty, are fined].
12.notes: an almost verbatim twin of 22:3, contrasting the arum (H6175) who reads danger and shelters with the peti (H6612) who blunders ahead. To see (raah, H7200) and hide is wisdom; to walk on heedless is to be fined (anash, H6064) by the consequence one refused to foresee.

13.text: Seize the coat of one who pledges himself for a stranger, and hold it as security when he stands surety for a foreign woman.
13.amp: Take [laqach — seize, hold] his garment [beged] that is surety [arab — has pledged, guaranteed] for a stranger [zur], and take a pledge [chabal] of him for a foreign woman [nokri].
13.notes: a near-repeat of 20:16, this is hard-edged practical wisdom: anyone reckless enough to pledge (arab, H6148) himself for a zur (H2114) or a nokri (H5237) is a poor credit risk, so demand his beged (H899) as collateral up front. Proverbs repeatedly warns against rash suretyship (cf. 6:1-5; 11:15).

14.text: Whoever blesses his neighbor with a booming voice, rising up early in the morning, will have it counted to him as a curse.
14.amp: He who blesses [barak] his friend [rea] with a loud [gadol — great, booming] voice [qol], rising early [shakam — getting up at dawn to do it] in the morning [boqer], it shall be counted [chashab — reckoned, accounted] a curse [qelalah] to him.
14.notes: a wry proverb on tactless excess: a blessing (barak, H1288) shouted too loud and too early is heard as its opposite, a qelalah (H7045) — the very curse it pretends to oppose. shakam (H7925), to rise early with eager zeal, here exposes a flattery so overdone it grates; chashab (H2803) means it gets 'reckoned' as the reverse of its intent.

15.text: A constant dripping on a day of steady rain and a quarrelsome wife are one and the same.
15.amp: A continual [tarad — driving on without stop] dropping [delef — a leak] in a very rainy [sagrir] day [yom] and a contentious [from madon — strife, quarreling] woman [ishshah] are alike [shavah — matched, equal].
15.notes: the maddening, unrelenting drip of a leaky roof (delef) on a soaking day is shavah (H7737) — set equal — to life with a quarrelsome wife: not a single blow but a wearing, ceaseless tarad (H2956). madon (H4066), strife, is the same word the book repeatedly ties to misery in the home (cf. 19:13; 21:9).

16.text: To restrain her is to restrain the wind, or to grasp oil with the right hand.
16.amp: Whoever hides [tsaphan — stores up, restrains] her hides [tsaphan] the wind [ruach], and the ointment [shemen — oil] of his right hand [yamin] betrays [qara — calls out, gives itself away] itself.
16.notes: the contentious wife of v.15 cannot be contained: to tsaphan (H6845) her — to store or hold her back — is to bottle the ruach (H7307), the wind, or to clutch oil that slips through the fingers and announces its escape. The image confesses the futility of trying to silence strife by force rather than peace.

17.text: Iron is sharpened by iron, and one man sharpens the face of his friend.
17.amp: Iron [barzel] sharpens [chadad — makes keen] iron [barzel]; so a man [ish] sharpens [chadad] the countenance [panim — face] of his friend [rea].
17.notes: the friction of barzel (H1270) on barzel — the doubled noun, the doubled verb chadad (H2300) — pictures two lives rubbed against each other until both come away keener. To sharpen a friend's panim (H6440), his face, is to sharpen his whole bearing and mind; real friendship is bracing, not merely soothing.

18.text: Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and whoever guards his master will be honored.
18.amp: Whoever keeps [natsar — tends, watches over] the fig tree [teenah] shall eat [akal] its fruit [peri]; so he who waits on [shamar — keeps, attends] his master [adon] shall be honored [kabad — be made weighty, glorified].
18.notes: the two keeping-verbs natsar (H5341) and shamar (H8104) bind the proverb together: as patient care for the teenah earns its fruit, so faithful service to one's adon (H113) earns honor. kabad (H3513), to be honored, is literally to be made 'weighty' — the reward of steady, loyal attention.

19.text: As water mirrors face to face, so a man's heart reveals the man.
19.amp: As in water [mayim] face [panim] answers to face [panim], so the heart [leb] of man [adam] to man [adam].
19.notes: as still water throws back the panim (H6440) that bends over it, the leb (H3820) — the inner self — shows a man what he truly is. The proverb can also read outward: in another's heart a man sees his own reflected, for human hearts answer one another like water answers a face.

20.text: Sheol and Abaddon are never full, and the eyes of man are never satisfied.
20.amp: Hell [sheol — the grave, the realm of the dead] and destruction [abaddon — the place of ruin, the abyss] are never full [sabea — sated, filled]; so the eyes [ayin] of man [adam] are never satisfied [sabea].
20.notes: the repeated sabea (H7646) ties two bottomless things together: as sheol (H7585) and abaddon (H10) swallow the dead without ever being filled, so the human ayin (H5869) — the eye, the seat of desire — forever craves more (cf. Eccl 1:8; 1 John 2:16). Covetousness is a grave that never closes.

21.text: The crucible tests silver and the furnace gold, and a man is tested by the praise he receives.
21.amp: As the fining pot [matsreph — the crucible] for silver [keseph], and the furnace [kur] for gold [zahav]; so is a man [ish] to his praise [mahalal — the praise given him, or by what he praises].
21.notes: as the matsreph (H4715) proves keseph and the furnace proves zahav, praise (mahalal, H4110) proves the man: how he handles applause — and what he himself praises — reveals the metal beneath. The same root halal that ran through vv.1-2 returns; honor is not only sought but a test of the one who receives it.

22.text: Though you grind a fool in a mortar with a pestle, among the crushed grain, his folly will not leave him.
22.amp: Though you should pound [a fool] in a mortar [maktesh — the hollow grinding-bowl] among [tavek — in the midst of] wheat [riphot — crushed grain] with a pestle, yet his foolishness [ivvelet — folly] will not depart [sur — turn aside, be removed] from him.
22.notes: the most violent image of incorrigibility in Proverbs: even crushed in the maktesh (H4388) like grain, the fool's ivvelet (H200) will not sur (H5493) — will not be ground out of him. Folly is not a surface stain but the substance of the man; no external force can remove what the heart refuses to surrender (cf. 26:11).

23.text: Know well the condition of your flocks, and set your heart upon your herds.
23.amp: Be diligent to know [yada — know intimately, attend to] the state [panim — the face, the condition] of your flocks [tson], and set [shith — place, fix] your heart [leb] to your herds [eder].
23.notes: the closing charge (vv.23-27) opens with yada (H3045), to know by close attention — a shepherd must know the panim (H6440), the very face, of his tson (H6629). 'Look well' is literally shith leb (H7896 + H3820), set the heart: diligent husbandry is an affair of the heart, not mere accounting.

24.text: For riches do not last forever, nor does a crown endure to every generation.
24.amp: For riches [chosen — stored wealth, strength] are not forever [olam]; and does the crown [nezer — the diadem, the mark of rank] endure to every generation [dor — age, generation, doubled: 'generation and generation']?
24.notes: the reason for diligence (v.23): chosen (H2633), hoarded wealth, is not olam (H5769), not everlasting, and even a nezer (H5145) — a crown — does not pass unbroken from dor to dor (H1755). Inherited fortune and rank are fragile; only steady, working stewardship feeds a house across the years.

25.text: When the grass is gone and the new growth appears, and the herbs of the hills are gathered in,
25.amp: The hay [chatsir] is removed [galah — uncovered, taken away], and the tender grass [deshe] shows [raah — appears] itself, and herbs [eseb — green plants] of the mountains [har] are gathered [asaph — collected, brought in].
25.notes: the proverb turns to the rhythm of the seasons: as galah (H1540) clears the old hay and fresh deshe appears, the eseb (H6212) of the hills is gathered (asaph, H622). The diligent shepherd of v.23 works with this God-given cycle, and provision follows in its turn (vv.26-27).

26.text: The lambs will clothe you, and the goats will buy you a field;
26.amp: The lambs [keves] are for your clothing [levush], and the goats [attud] are the price [mechir — the purchase-money] of a field [sadeh].
26.notes: the reward of careful husbandry made concrete: the keves yield levush (H3830), clothing, and the attud become the mechir (H4242), the price, of a sadeh (H7704), a field. Faithful tending of the flock turns into wool on the back and land underfoot — wealth that grows from work, not from hoarding (v.24).

27.text: and there will be goats' milk enough for your own food, for the food of your household, and to sustain the life of your servant girls.
27.amp: And you shall have goats' milk [chalav] enough for your food [lechem — bread, sustenance], for the food [lechem] of your household [bayith], and for the maintenance [chay — life, livelihood] of your maidens [naarah — young servant women].
27.notes: the book's domestic vision closes in plenty: chalav (H2461), milk, feeds the master, his bayith (H1004), and even his naarah (H5291) servants. The word for their 'maintenance' is chay (H2416), life itself — diligent stewardship is finally about sustaining lives, a whole household provided for from a well-tended flock.
